source.title: SAT: Improving Adversarial Training via Curriculum-Based Loss Smoothing
source.authors: Chawin Sitawarin; Supriyo Chakraborty; David A. Wagner

record.tranche_reason: The study reports adversarial-training results and adversarial generalization gaps. It does not test the listed versions about natural-label generalization or the specified magnitude-aware sharpness measure.
record.gate_note: The reported generalization gaps are for adversarial accuracy, so they do not establish whether networks trained on natural labels generalize as the claim describes. The paper's clean/adversarial accuracy comparisons are not train/test-gap measurements.
record.test_reason: The study measures curriculum-based adversarial training, adversarial accuracy gaps, and Hessian/gradient smoothness. It does not test any listed version. In particular, it does not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or compare its ranking with norm- and margin-based measures. Its reliance on a broader flatness–generalization hypothesis does not establish use or testing of that specific claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: they argue that curriculum-based loss smoothing improves clean accuracy and adversarial generalization, and that H-SAT and P-SAT outperform compared defenses in most settings. This is their stated conclusion; individual accuracy comparisons are mixed, and their claimed agreement between Hessian and generalization-gap orderings contradicts the reported H-SAT/P-SAT numbers.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses curriculum-based adversarial training, comparing Hessian- and probability-based variants with adversarial-training baselines; its reported generalization gaps concern adversarial accuracy.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that the three smoothness measures change trend around epoch 40, when the learning rate is reduced. It also reports different adversarial-gap values across AT, H-SAT, and P-SAT.

fits_no_version.finding: On CIFAR-10 at epsilon 8/255, adversarial accuracy gaps are 2.42 ± 0.18 percentage points for AT, 2.08 ± 0.21 for H-SAT, and 2.33 ± 0.24 for P-SAT. Both SAT variants have smaller point estimates than AT. However, P-SAT has the smallest Hessian eigenvalue and trace, whereas H-SAT has the smallest gap. The authors' assertion of matching orderings is therefore inconsistent with their reported numbers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this adversarial-training comparison, SAT variants have lower Hessian smoothness measures and smaller adversarial generalization-gap point estimates than AT, but Hessian measures do not reproduce the gap ranking between H-SAT and P-SAT.

fits_no_version.finding: After epoch 40, gradient norms rank H-SAT lowest, P-SAT next, and AT highest, matching the reported adversarial-gap point estimates. These are gradient norms rather than magnitude-aware sharpness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-norm and adversarial-gap rankings agree across these three training schemes in the reported CIFAR-10 setting.

record.problems: The reported generalization-gap comparison is for CIFAR-10 at one perturbation norm and one architecture. The Hessian and gradient comparisons are described qualitatively and shown in figures without extracted numerical values. The paper's adversarial-accuracy gap is not the natural-label gap in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: Clean/adversarial accuracy tables compare defense performance but do not measure the train/test gap. Other datasets and perturbation settings lack the reported train/test-gap measurement described in Section 6.2.3.

untested.parts: Paired random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and training recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Controlled adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparisons of held-out performance and tuning scope.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance. Changing batch size only for Hessian approximation does not test this.
Dropout effects on held-out error, including training-set size and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps at similarly low training loss, and its ranking relative to norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Adversarial training alone does not exclude a study from testing these versions; the decisive issue here is the absence of the specified comparisons and measures. No statistical significance of the differences between adversarial gaps is established by the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test accuracy.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and natural-label test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD on held-out performance.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbations and their ranking of natural train/test gaps; the paper reports different smoothness measurements in adversarial training.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: AT, H-SAT, and P-SAT, PreAct-ResNet-20
rows.operation_detail: Compared maximal Hessian eigenvalue on adversarial examples generated by PGD during training; the paper describes the post-epoch-40 trend qualitatively.
rows.measure: Maximal Hessian eigenvalue as a loss-smoothness measure
rows.baseline: AT is described as having the largest value among the three after epoch 40.
rows.note: The text describes the ordering but gives no numerical values. The measure is not magnitude-aware weight perturbation.
rows.check: The qualitative ordering is explicitly stated in Section 6.2.3, so the evidence is not figure-only. Maximal Hessian eigenvalue is not V7's magnitude-aware sharpness. This is a comparison of the study's training methods.

rows.baseline: AT is described as largest after epoch 40; H-SAT and P-SAT switch order compared with the Hessian measures.
rows.value: The general trend remains the same; H-SAT and P-SAT switch places.
rows.note: The text gives no numerical values for this comparison.
rows.check: Section 6.2.3 explicitly gives the ordering: H-SAT has the smallest gradient norm, P-SAT the next smallest, and AT the largest after epoch 40. The evidence is not figure-only. Gradient norm measures none of the listed versions.
